chunks: And that which was narrated is: Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Fadhl from 'Amr ibn Sa'id al-Mada'ini from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from 'Ammar al-Sabati who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who sets out for his own need, and he does not intend travel, so he continues in that and his walking extends until he covers eight farsakhs. What should he do regarding his prayer? He said: 'He shortens (the prayer) and does not complete it until he returns to his home.'

The ruling regarding it is that it becomes obligatory upon him to shorten after crossing eight farsakhs until he returns to his home, because he has become a traveler, even if he did not intend that from the beginning. And the first narration only included the obligation of completion during the duration of his walking for the mentioned amount, and they are not contradictory on this basis. If a person sets out traveling and travels two farsakhs and shortens, then returns to his intention (of being a resident), if he had shortened in the prayer he must repeat the prayer. That which indicates this is what was narrated:

key_terms.التَّقْصِيرُ: Shortening the prayer (performing 2 rak'ahs instead of 4)
key_terms.فَرَاسِخَ: Farsakhs (a unit of distance, approx 4-6 km)

ai.seo_question: What is the prayer ruling for someone who travels eight farsakhs without initially intending to be a traveler?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the Shia juristic principle that the status of *musafir* (traveler) is determined by the actual distance covered rather than initial intention, specifically establishing eight *farsakhs* as the threshold for obligatory prayer shortening (*qasr*). Scholars note that this ruling applies even if the journey was incidental, distinguishing it from cases where one returns before reaching the distance, thereby resolving apparent contradictions in earlier narrations regarding the duration of travel status.
